newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuban spy master says Che wanted more revolutions.
newsitem.headline: Cuban spy master says Che wanted more revolutions.

text.p: Legendary guerrilla fighter Ernesto "Che" Guevara always wanted to move on from Cuba to lead struggles in other countries, Cuban spy master Manuel Pineiro said in a rare interview published on Thursday.

Pineiro, who formerly ran Cuba's secret operations in support of armed leftist groups in Latin America, said Guevara left Cuba with a child-like enthusiasm to continue what he viewed as his life's work as a revolutionary.
Guevara, an Argentine doctor, became Fidel Castro's right-hand man in the guerrilla struggle that led to the 1959 revolution that ushered in a Communist government in Cuba.
After holding several leadership posts, including president of Cuba's central bank, Guevara took off to fight in the Congo and Bolivia, where he was captured and executed in 1967.
Just before setting out for Bolivia to lead an abortive uprising, Guevara was like "a child with a new toy," Pineiro told the July edition of the Cuban magazine Tricontinental.

Pineiro said that even before the launch of the Castro's rebel struggle in 1956, Guevara "told Fidel that as soon as he could free himself from his responsibilities with the Cuban revolution and the time was right, he wanted to have the freedom to join the revolutionary struggle in another Latin American country, preferably Argentina."

Guevara, an inspiration for a generation of leftists around the world, left Cuba in 1965 to try to export Cuba's revolution, first in the Congo in Africa and then in Bolivia, where he was caught and shot by Bolivian troops.

Guevara's bones were unearthed from a secret mass grave in Bolivia earlier this month and returned to Cuba. He will be buried in a mausoleum in the central town of Santa Clara in October, the 30th anniversary of his death.

Pineiro, nicknamed "Red Beard," headed Cuba's intelligence service in the 1960s and Cuban efforts to foster revolution in Latin America. He portrayed Guevara as impatient to move on from Cuba, and Castro as supportive but anxious to hold him back from danger.
Some historians have suggested that Guevara's departure was due to a falling-out with Castro.
Guevara wanted to go in at the start of a failed mission led by Argentine journalist Jorge Ricardo Masetti to begin a revolution in Argentina in 1963, Pineiro said.

"Fidel persuaded him to enter Argentina only when an advance party had created the right conditions, that he shouldn't be there in the most difficult and risky stage of any guerrilla movement, that of survival," he said.
When most of those who took part in this mission died or disappeared in 1964, Guevara was bothered by the "idea that while this was happening, he was in an office," Pineiro added.

When Guevara started planning the Bolivian uprising, Castro again tried to persuade him he should not go until the struggle was successfully underway, but Guevara was anxious to start fighting, Pineiro said.
"He felt very compelled by the passage of time. He knew better than anyone that to be in good physical shape was absolutely necessary to lead a guerrilla movement," he added.
He said Guevara wanted to strike before the United States succeeded in thwarting the spread of "the example of the Cuban revolution" to other parts of Latin America.
